134: ≈ 0.8 µm across here, but up to tens of centimetres long (only a nearby collateral is drawn). No rough ER: everything comes from the soma. Microtubules all oriented + end towards the terminal, neurofilaments, periodic actin rings (≈ 190 nm). Beyond the initial segment, the myelin sheath (not drawn) allows saltatory conduction.
135: The receiving pole of the neuron. Microtubules of mixed orientation (MAP2), mitochondria, smooth ER, Golgi outposts and polysomes at the foot of spines: mRNAs (CaMKIIα, Arc) are translated on the spot, close to active synapses. Each spine (bulges visible through the membrane) usually receives one excitatory synapse; a pyramidal neuron bears about 10,000. The dendrite continues beyond the dark disc (not drawn).
137: Presynaptic terminal: one to a few hundred synaptic vesicles, a handful of them docked at the active zone (dark disc) facing the spine. When the action potential arrives, Ca²⁺ channels (Cav2.1) open; synaptotagmin-1 senses Ca²⁺ and the SNARE complex (syntaxin-1, SNAP-25, synaptobrevin-2) fuses a vesicle in under a millisecond. The membrane is then recycled by endocytosis.
139: ≈ 40 nm in diameter. Its V-ATPase builds a proton gradient that the transporter VGLUT1 uses to fill it with glutamate (≈ 1,500 to 2,000 molecules). It carries ≈ 70 synaptobrevins, ≈ 30 synaptophysins, ≈ 15 synaptotagmins, ≈ 10 Rab3A and only one or two V-ATPases.
140: Dendritic spine of a neighbouring neuron
141: A ≈ 0.5 µm head on a narrow neck. Under its membrane, the postsynaptic density (dark disc): the PSD-95 scaffold holds the glutamate receptors AMPA (fast depolarisation) and NMDA (Ca²⁺ entry only if the membrane is already depolarised: a coincidence detector). Insertion or removal of AMPA receptors underlies long-term potentiation and depression. The synaptic cleft is ≈ 20 nm wide.
143: You are floating in an erythroblastic island. The cell in front of you is a basophilic erythroblast (≈16 µm), a still nucleated red cell precursor. The small bilobed proteins are holo-transferrins (80 kDa), each carrying 2 Fe³⁺ ions.
145: A phospholipid bilayer about 5 nm thick, several million lipids per µm². Asymmetric: phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin on the outer side, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine on the cytosolic side, rich in cholesterol. Impermeable to ions and macromolecules: you need a receptor to get in.
147: Transmembrane homodimer (2 × 95 kDa, disulfide bonds). Each dimer binds two holo-transferrins with nanomolar affinity. The erythroblast displays several hundred thousand of them to capture iron for haem. Land on the flagged pit (size ≤ 30 nm).
148: The adaptor AP-2 recognises the YTRF motif of the TfR1 tail and recruits clathrin. Triskelia (3 heavy + 3 light chains) assemble into a cage of pentagons and hexagons that bends the membrane.
149: A very crowded aqueous gel: 200–300 g/L of protein. pH ≈ 7.2; K⁺ ≈ 140 mM, Na⁺ ≈ 10 mM, free Ca²⁺ ≈ 100 nM. In the erythroblast it gradually fills with haemoglobin. The beige grains are free polysomes. Avoid the organelles!
150: Several 80S ribosomes (25–30 nm; 4 rRNAs and ≈80 proteins; 40S and 60S subunits) translate the same mRNA at ≈5 amino acids per second. Their abundance makes the cytoplasm basophilic: they mostly make α and β globins, cytosolic proteins (hence not on the ER).
151: Two membranes: the outer one is permeable (VDAC porins); the inner one, folded into cristae, carries the respiratory chain and ATP synthase (proton gradient). Matrix: Krebs cycle, β-oxidation, circular mitochondrial DNA of 16,569 bp (37 genes, maternally inherited; yellow dots). Here it also makes haem: ALAS2 opens the pathway in the matrix, ferrochelatase ends it by inserting Fe²⁺ into protoporphyrin IX. Iron enters through mitoferrin-1.
152: Flattened cisternae (lumen ≈50 nm) continuous with the outer nuclear membrane, covered with ribosomes docked on the Sec61 translocon. Synthesis of membrane and secreted proteins (including TfR1), folding (BiP, calnexin), disulfide bonds, N-glycosylation.
153: A network of tubules ≈60 nm in diameter (reticulons; three-way junctions formed by atlastins). Synthesis of phospholipids and cholesterol, Ca²⁺ store (≈0.5 mM versus 100 nM in the cytosol), contacts with mitochondria.
154: A polarised stack of 4 to 6 cisternae: cis face (arrival of COPII vesicles from the ER) → medial cisternae → trans face and trans-Golgi network (sorting). N-glycan maturation, O-glycosylation, sulfation. Mannose-6-phosphate tag for lysosomal enzymes; return to the ER in COPI vesicles.
155: Two perpendicular centrioles (9 microtubule triplets, ≈0.2 × 0.45 µm) in a pericentriolar material where γ-tubulin rings nucleate microtubules. Duplicated only once per cycle, in S phase.
156: A hollow 25 nm tube: 13 protofilaments of α/β-tubulin dimers (8 nm). Polarised: − end at the centrosome, + end at the periphery, with dynamic instability (GTP hydrolysis). Track for kinesins (towards +) and dynein (towards −).
158: A membrane sac of 50–100 nm. The moving ones are hauled along a microtubule by a kinesin: 8 nm steps, 1 ATP per step, ≈1 µm/s (real speed here). Addressing by Rab GTPases, fusion by SNAREs.
159: pH 4.5–5 maintained by the V-ATPase; about sixty acid hydrolases digest proteins, lipids, sugars and nucleic acids (endocytosis, autophagy). Membrane protected by LAMP glycoproteins. An enzyme deficiency = a lysosomal storage disease.
160: Single membrane, no DNA. β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, plasmalogen synthesis; catalase destroys H₂O₂ here. Proteins are imported already folded (PTS1 signal “-SKL”, PEX peroxins).
162: Tubulo-vesicular sorting compartment (pH ≈ 6, Rab5). This is where iron leaves transferrin; receptors return to the surface through recycling tubules (Rab4, Rab11).
163: ESCRT complexes bud ≈50 nm vesicles inwards, loaded with receptors to be eliminated. It fuses with a lysosome — or with the plasma membrane, releasing exosomes: this is how the reticulocyte gets rid of TfR1.
165: Two bilayers separated by the perinuclear space (30–50 nm), joined at the rim of each pore. The outer one continues the ER and bears ribosomes; the inner one has its own proteins (LBR, emerin, LAP2, MAN1, SUN1/2) and rests on the lamina. At each mitosis CDK1 phosphorylates lamins and nucleoporins: the envelope comes apart, then re-forms around the chromosomes in telophase.
167: ≈110–120 MDa, about thirty nucleoporins with 8-fold symmetry: cytoplasmic, inner and nuclear rings, cytoplasmic filaments, nuclear basket. Outer diameter ≈120 nm; central channel ≈40 nm filled with disordered FG nucleoporins. Free diffusion up to ≈40 kDa; beyond that, importins/exportins and the Ran-GTP gradient. The ship must be ≤ 40 nm.
169: Interchromatin channels where RNAs, transcription factors and splicing factors diffuse. 46 decondensed chromosomes (interphase): 6.1 billion base pairs, i.e. ≈2 m of DNA in an 8 µm nucleus.
170: Each chromosome is one continuous fibre folded within its own territory (1 node per megabase, schematic folding). Shades follow the G bands when the UCSC API responds: light = gene-rich R bands, dark = G bands, red = centromere. Gene-rich chromosomes (17, 19, 22) tend to lie at the centre of the nucleus, gene-poor ones (4, 13, 18) at the periphery.
